title: Why Cooperation Is Essential in Crisis - IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Why Cooperation Is Essential in Crisis - IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.docx

speakers: Nicolai Tangen (CEO, Norges Bank Investment Management, host)
summary:
Interview (Dec 2025) with the IMF head on the institution's role, the state of the world economy, tariffs, debt, inflation, climate and AI.
She sees growth resilient at about 3% thanks to stronger institutions, agile private sectors and a smaller-than-feared trade shock, but argues debt leaves no buffers.
AI is seen as profitable but with stretched valuations, a likely partial correction, and large labor-market and inequality effects.

coverage.note: IMF mandate, lending capacity, data, Bulgaria currency board, Argentina programs, World Bank split
IMF governance and funding, state of world economy: growth about 3% vs 3.7% pre-COVID
three reasons for resilience, tariff levels, no retaliation, debt and fiscal buffers, US deficit
disinflation and tariff pass-through, climate as financial risk, AI preparedness index, growth and jobs impact
AI inequality, cooperation at the IMF, AI investment justified by profits
AI valuation correction view, decarbonization setback, climate in country programs, IMF scope
COVID lending and SDR response, coordination, personal background
biography and personal advice only, nothing actionable

completeness_estimate: 0.90 - first reader captured essentially all macro content (growth, tariffs, debt, inflation, climate, AI, COVID response); gaps are IMF institutional facts, the US veto, Europe inflation and a few small policy remarks. C08 is biography only.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: we have this unique right to collect data from all countries and we do that regularly
claims.claim: The IMF has a unique right to collect economic data from all 191 members, giving it a consistent global view (Article IV consultations, vital signs of economies).
claims.indicator: IMF member country data / Article IV

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: help us put in place a currency board which really stabilized the uh economy and put fiscal discipline
claims.claim: A currency board plus fiscal discipline ended Bulgaria's late-1990s hyperinflation (over 8,000%) and left debt at 24% of GDP, a historical example of stabilizing programs.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: Argentina has had a number of programs. So far, none of them got the country completely out of trouble.
claims.claim: Argentina has had many IMF programs without lasting recovery; the current program under a reform-minded president is hoped to be the last.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: We are projecting over 3% growth this year and next.
claims.claim: The IMF projects global growth just over 3% in 2025 and 2026, below the 3.7% pre-COVID average, resilient but too slow.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: we don't quite know how this multiple forces of transformation may test it in the future
claims.claim: The world economy's resilience has not been fully tested against geopolitics, technology, demography and climate together.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: countries have built stronger institutions and they have put in place sound policies
claims.claim: Reason one for resilience: since the financial crisis countries have independent central banks, fiscal rules and better tax systems, which cushion shocks.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: they bought goods before the tariffs hit so they can cushion their uh businesses
claims.claim: Reason two: a more agile private sector adapts to shocks, e.g. front-loading imports before tariffs.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: So on April 2nd the total announced tariffs were around 23%. When we look at the level now 17 18%.
claims.claim: Announced US tariffs fell from about 23% in April 2025 to 17-18%, and actually collected tariffs are only 8-9%, so the trade shock is smaller than feared.
claims.indicator: effective US tariff rate, customs collections

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: We worried that all countries would say me too.
claims.claim: Tit-for-tat retaliation did not occur; if it had, the negative impact on global growth would have been much larger.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: Because uh servicing debt especially when interest rates are no more zero or even negative takes away money from other productive purposes.
claims.claim: High debt with positive interest rates crowds out productive spending (infrastructure, AI readiness, education).

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: because when you have very high level of debt, you really have no buffers.
claims.claim: With high debt there is no fiscal or monetary space for the next shock, unlike COVID, so gradual consolidation is advised.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: when countries put in place various programs to support people and businesses and they don't need them anymore it's very difficult to take them back
claims.claim: Emergency support programs are hard to withdraw, creating a ratchet in deficits.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: He thinks that they need to bring down the deficit to 3%.
claims.claim: IMF and US Treasury Secretary Bessent agree the US deficit should be brought down to about 3% of GDP.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: We see the uh trend in disinflation continuing in the right direction.
claims.claim: Global disinflation continues, but US tariff effects on prices have been muted so far, so the IMF is not yet declaring victory.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: Two because companies profitable they could eat up some of the tariffs.
claims.claim: Tariff pass-through to consumer prices has been delayed by pre-positioned inventory and by profitable companies absorbing part of tariffs; the future path is unknown.
claims.conditions: may reverse as inventories run down

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: if you accumulate in your portfolio assets that are vulnerable either to cl climate shocks or to change in policy, then you can see um unexpected significant losses on your on your assets
claims.claim: Climate is a financial risk through climate-vulnerable assets and policy changes, and through vulnerable communities (e.g. Philippines, Vietnam).

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: we created an index on AI preparedness that ranks 174 countries on four things.
claims.claim: The IMF AI Preparedness Index (digital infrastructure, labor flexibility/skills, innovation, regulation/ethics) shows advanced economies (Singapore, Denmark, US) ready and most developing countries not.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: somewhere between 0.1 and 0.8% 8% of additional growth
claims.claim: The IMF estimates AI could add 0.1 to 0.8 percentage points of extra global growth, a large amount given slow growth.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: over the next couple of years in rich countries 60% of jobs will be impacted by AI
claims.claim: About 60% of jobs in rich countries, 40% globally and 26% in low-income countries will be affected by AI (enhanced, changed or eliminated), a labor-market tsunami.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: both within countries and across countries we may see divergence because of AI
claims.claim: AI risks widening inequality within and between countries, since only prepared economies capture the gains.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: Since we got into a more geopolitically confrontational world, I see in my work at the IMF more appetite to cooperate.
claims.claim: Geopolitical confrontation has increased the IMF members' appetite to cooperate, since cooperation can no longer be taken for granted.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: In other words, this increase in investment is justified by uh profitability.
claims.claim: AI investment is supported by actual profits of AI firms, which argues against a pure bubble.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: likely uh some yes, just because enthusiasm has pushed valuations that are now so stretched
claims.claim: A correction in AI-related valuations is likely because enthusiasm has stretched valuations, but not a very bad outcome since AI is producing marketable, profitable products.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: if there is one issue that AI creates, it's not so much the stretch valuations, it is a departure from a path towards decarbonization
claims.claim: AI's energy demand threatens to pull countries off the decarbonization path, a larger issue than valuations.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: when is climate a factor in macroeconomic and financial uh stability and when it is we have to take it into account
claims.claim: Climate shocks must be built into budget plans of exposed countries such as Jamaica, as the IMF treats climate as a macro-financial factor when material.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: We deployed about a trillion dollars in lending and through the allocation of special drawing right 650 billion injection in reserves
claims.claim: In COVID the IMF deployed about $1tn in lending plus $650bn of SDR reserves, giving countries a floor.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: that was done in a coordinated manner makes a huge difference whether individual countries do their individual thing or the world comes together with a strong uh coordinated uh response
claims.claim: Coordinated monetary and fiscal responses make a large difference compared with each country acting alone.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: We have lending capacity of $1 trillion. We deploy it for countries in crisis.
claims.claim: The IMF's role is to lend quickly (capacity about $1 trillion) to finance balance-of-payments needs of countries in crisis, not to fund investment projects, so it acts as a cushion that stops a country 'about to crash'.
claims.conditions: when markets close to a country or reserves run out

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: The best value from the fund is to put in place good policies and responsible institutions.
claims.claim: The IMF argues the lasting benefit comes from good policies and responsible institutions that let a country grow on its own after the emergency cushion, rather than from repeated bailouts.
claims.direction: better institutions lead to a better growth trajectory
claims.conditions: countries that implement the reforms attached to programs
claims.testable: partly - program outcomes can be compared but selection is severe

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: We are like a savings bank. Countries commit resources to the fund. Then we lend this money.
claims.claim: The IMF is funded by member quotas that it lends out and is repaid with interest, with no taxpayer contributions, which lets it commit large sums very quickly in a crisis.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: they hold over 17% of the quarters of the IMF and in that sense they are the only member that has v2 power
claims.claim: The US holds over 17% of IMF quotas and so is the only member with a veto, because major decisions require at least 85% of the vote; global crisis support therefore depends on US consent.

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: Europe has done a very good job in bringing inflation to target.
claims.claim: Inflation in Europe is back at target, while US disinflation is slower and exposed to tariff pass-through, so the IMF sees the inflation threat as more contained in Europe.
claims.testable: yes - compare inflation prints with targets

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: financial stability risks that are related to either the economy changing rapidly uh which by the way seems to be now a slower process to decarbonization
claims.claim: Climate-related financial stability risk has a transition channel (rapid economic change) and a physical channel (shocks to businesses and households); the transition channel looks smaller now because decarbonization is proceeding more slowly.
claims.testable: partly - transition risk scenarios can be stress-tested

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: countries that have the um comparative advantage, cheap energy, preferably renewable energy, um high level of investment in research and development, they have responsibility to move the frontier
claims.claim: Countries with cheap (preferably renewable) energy and high R&D investment have the comparative advantage to push the AI frontier, which links AI capacity to energy cost and research spending.
claims.direction: AI leadership favors cheap-energy, high-R&D economies
claims.testable: partly - cross-country AI investment against energy cost and R&D

claims.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva
claims.quote: what is um different today is that getting uh cooperation uh takes more more effort
claims.claim: Coordinated crisis response is harder to assemble now than in COVID, when emergency meetings produced a fast joint response, so the next shock may meet a slower and less coordinated policy reaction, especially with no fiscal buffers.
